title: Phantom Blade Zero Combat System - Sha-chi, Blades & Phantom Edges
description: How Phantom Blade Zero combat works: the Sha-chi resource, two blade slots plus two Phantom Edges, power surge abilities, and a progression system with no XP. Based on confirmed information only.
keyword: phantom blade zero combat system sha-chi

sections.title: Combat Overview
sections.content:
Phantom Blade Zero is an action RPG that sits between two traditions. It borrows the interconnected level design and oppressive atmosphere associated with Souls games, while taking its combat feel from fast character-action titles like Devil May Cry, Ninja Gaiden and Metal Gear Rising. S-GAME has been explicit that calling it a "soulslike" undersells what it is doing.

The studio's own framing is "Kung Fu Punk": Chinese martial arts choreography combined with modern and punk visual elements, set in a universe called the Phantom World.

Remnant Dust is the principal currency, per the October 2026 studio preview, and it is what you spend on weapon upgrades after reforging returns your materials. That is the mechanical answer to a boss you cannot beat: the preview describes the loop as rethinking the fight rather than grinding past it. Some of that is elemental - the same coverage describes countering a flame-breathing opponent with a jetstream of water, which is a Phantom Edge choice rather than a stat problem.

sections.title: Sha-chi: The Central Resource
sections.content:
Sha-chi is the combat resource that drives the game's offence and defence. It is spent on Sha-chi attacks — heavy attacks — and on blocking.

This is the single most important thing to understand about the combat before you play: there is no separate stamina bar to manage. Sha-chi is the pool that gates your heavier options, so how you generate and spend it shapes every encounter.

SystemDetail
Combat resourceSha-chi
Spent onHeavy (Sha-chi) attacks, blocking
Stamina barNo separate stamina bar in the traditional sense — Sha-chi fills that role
Level-upsNo XP-based levelling

sections.title: What Actually Drains The Bar
sections.content:
The single most common misreading of this combat is that Sha-chi is a stamina bar you spend on strong attacks. Community documentation lists four separate drains, and only one of them is your own aggression:

  • Taking damage - getting hit costs you the resource, so a bad exchange is a double loss.
  • Holding stance (架势) - the guard posture burns Sha-chi continuously while auto-blocking most attacks and chipping the enemy's own bar.
  • Auto-blocking - including the forced block against white-glow attacks described below.
  • Sha-chi attacks - your heavy attacks, the only attacks that reduce an enemy's bar.

It recovers on its own once you stop spending it for a moment, and an enemy blocking your attacks drains their bar too. That is the whole puzzle: normal attacks cannot touch an enemy's Sha-chi, but making them block can. Sustained pressure with ordinary swings is a resource play, not just damage.

Normal attacks cost nothing and cannot reduce the enemy bar; Sha-chi attacks do both, and some weapons gain extra effects when the bar is high. Weapon choice changes this calculus per blade.

sections.title: Guard Break Is The Real Loss Condition
sections.content:
When either Sha-chi bar empties, that side is 破防 - guard-broken. While broken you cannot hold stance, cannot use Sha-chi-consuming techniques, take increased damage, and are held in a long stagger with your animations interrupted. The enemy cannot block during their own break, which is the window you are trying to create.

The escape is specific and worth memorising before launch: switching main weapons instantly cancels guard break and refills the bar, at the cost of putting the outgoing weapon on cooldown. The same swap is what lets you drop out of a broken state mid-fight rather than eating the stagger.

One more trap: some enemies adopt their own guard posture, and attacking them while they hold it triggers a throw or grab counter. Long attacks into a stance-holding enemy are how runs actually end.

Flagged as a correction. A machine-generated wiki circulating in this niche claims weapon-switching refills Sha-chi, and it was reasonable to read that as invented. The BWIKI combat page states the same mechanic with the cooldown caveat attached, so treat the switch-back refill as community-reported rather than fabricated. It has still not been confirmed by S-GAME.

Why older coverage says "stamina". IGN watched the 2024 demo and reported that switching weapons restored stamina instantly and let an ongoing combo keep running. The BWIKI combat page, written against 2026 footage, describes the same input as refilling the Sha-chi bar, adding that the outgoing weapon goes on cooldown. The coherent reading is one meter under two names - Sha-chi already does the work a stamina bar would, since it governs both heavy attacks and blocking - with the 2026 build attaching a cost the 2024 build did not. Neither source says this. It is an inference, and it is the kind that breaks: if the retail game ships a separate stamina meter, or if the combo-continuation survived as its own property, this paragraph is wrong. It will be corrected against the shipped build.

sections.title: White, Red And Black Glow
sections.content:
Enemy attacks are colour-coded, and the correct answer differs per colour. Community documentation gives three rules and one open question:

  • White glow (白光) - blocking it works but burns a large amount of Sha-chi and leaves you in a stagger. A precise guard costs you nothing, takes the enemy's bar, and triggers Ghost Step.
  • Red glow (红光) - unblockable. Dodging precisely triggers Ghost Step with a large Sha-chi refund; some enemies go into a dedicated animation and a prompt-based sequence.
  • Black glow (黑光) - blocking it costs an enormous amount of Sha-chi. Whether a precisely-timed block helps is explicitly listed as unconfirmed.

Ghost Step (鬼步) is the reward loop: triggered by a precise guard on white or a precise dodge on red, it moves Soul behind the enemy, and the follow-up attack from there cannot be blocked and hits hard. So the defensive options are not defensive - they are the fastest way to build an uncounterable attack.

There is no published list of which enemies use which colour. Learn the three reflexes rather than the matchup table.

sections.title: Stealth And Executions
sections.content:
Combat can be started rather than entered. Crouching puts Soul in a stealth state; from behind an unaware ordinary enemy you get an execution, and when two ordinary enemies stand close together a single approach triggers a chained execution across both. Dropping onto an enemy from above while unseen also executes.

That matters more here than in most action games because of the surrounding systems: defeated enemies do not simply repopulate when you rest, so clearing a camp by stealth saves a real fight later, and kills probabilistically refund flask charges and feed the resource Phantom Edges consume.

The equipment-slot counts, the Sha-chi consumption list, the attack-colour rules and the stealth-execution behaviour on this page come from the 影之刃 WIKI on BWIKI (战斗系统 page, last edited 2026-10-13), a fan wiki run by the moderators of the 影之刃 Baidu Tieba with no affiliation to S-GAME. It is a pre-release compilation from footage, not a first-party document, so treat every number here as reported rather than confirmed. The official English statements on this page come from S-GAME and the publisher listings.

sections.title: A Naming Problem Worth Knowing About
sections.content:
English and Chinese material currently use resource names that do not line up, and this will confuse anyone comparing footage across regions.

The official English product page and the October studio preview call Remnant Dust the principal currency, spent on weapon upgrades, with the pre-order Treasure Basin raising its drop rate by 10%. The Chinese combat page describes two different things: 残魂星火, consumed to use Phantom Edges and gained probabilistically from kills - and 意识尘埃, spent on weapon upgrades alongside 金属 and 溶剂.

Neither mapping is clean. 残魂星火 reads back as "remnant-soul spark", so it fits the "Remnant" half of Remnant Dust but not the "dust" half; 意识尘埃 means "consciousness dust", so it fits "dust" but not "Remnant". Either the official English collapsed two resources into one name, or one of these terms is a fan translation. Do not assume they are the same item until a bilingual retail listing says so.

sections.title: Blades and Phantom Edges
sections.content:
The player character Soul fights with a two-slot weapon structure: primary weapons and secondary weapons.

Primary: Blades

Blades are the primary weapons. Each blade has a Power Surge, which functions as that weapon's ultimate ability. Rather than being flat stat sticks, blades carry distinct movesets and their own progression.

Secondary: Phantom Edges

Phantom Edges are the secondary weapons, and this is where the game's range broadens considerably. They include cannons, lances, axes, hammers and similar armaments. The player can carry two primary weapons and two secondary weapons, and can switch weapons mid-combo to extend attack chains.

On weapon counts: some sites state precise figures such as "30+ blades and 20+ Phantom Edges". S-GAME has not confirmed exact counts, and they can only be verified once the game ships. Treat specific numbers as unconfirmed.

sections.title: Progression Without XP
sections.content:
Phantom Blade Zero does not use a traditional experience-point levelling system. Instead, the character grows through equipment and found items:

  • Acquiring weapons and upgrading them
  • Finding items that raise your health and stamina gauges
  • Gear, artifacts and skills discovered through the game's optional challenges

The practical consequence is that exploration is progression. Seeking out the harder optional encounters is how you become stronger, rather than farming encounters for XP.

The Chinese combat page names the progression layer 能力修行 - ability cultivation - and states plainly that the numbers it publishes are post-upgrade figures, which is why some pre-release claims about fixed damage values should be read with suspicion. Related: weapon upgrades cap at 30 levels per BWIKI and can be reset with no loss, so a build is not a permanent commitment.

Growth is still equipment- and exploration-driven rather than XP-driven: Memory Flowers raise health and Sha-chi Amber raises the bar cap, which is where the "no levelling system" claim on this page comes from.

sections.title: The Motion Capture Approach
sections.content:
One production detail has a direct effect on how combat feels. S-GAME brought in Kenji Tanigaki as action director — a veteran martial arts fight choreographer with a long filmography.

Rather than using motion capture alone, Tanigaki physically demonstrated each move so it could be scanned with a camera matrix, after which animators rebuilt the movements by hand. The studio's position is that motion capture by itself could not do the choreography justice.

S-GAME has also motion captured real martial artists and performers for specific content — including visiting a Chinese dragon dance studio and turning that choreography into a boss fight.

sections.title: Where the Fighting Happens
sections.content:
The game unfolds in a semi-open world made up of multiple large, handcrafted maps rather than a single continuous open world. S-GAME has described the world as bleak and punishing by design — a setting that constantly discourages letting your guard down.

Exploration rewards weapons, armour, artifacts and skills. That loop is deliberate: because there is no XP system, the loot you find is your character progression.

See the protagonist and story premise for why the world is framed this way, or the beginner guide for how the pieces fit together.

Prefer to watch a fight rather than read it? Our boss video guide index lists third-party walkthroughs as plain links, with notes on which phases each one covers.
